book_title: Chapter 6: Eight Years in Numbers — From Distress to Scale, and the Cash Test Ahead
question: What does the full FY19–Sep 2026 financial record reveal about Jyoti CNC's cyclicality, capital efficiency, and balance-sheet trajectory?

epigraph.quote: A single boom year can flatter any P&L; eight years of balance sheets and cash flows tell you whether the business compounds or merely cycles.
epigraph.author: Long-Horizon Accounting Principle

web_blocks.html: Reviewing Jyoti CNC Automation across eight full years (FY19 through FY26, plus H1/TTM Sep 2026) strips away quarterly noise [1]. It reveals the company's true financial character [1]. The record splits cleanly into two distinct regimes [1]. First came the FY20–FY23 downcycle, with four straight net losses totaling ₹180 crore, OPM falling to 1.0% in FY20, and debt peaking at ₹835 crore [1]. Second came the FY24–FY26 post-IPO expansion, as sales jumped from ₹929 crore to ₹2,093 crore, OPM hit 25–27%, and ROCE reached 21.3% [1].

The 13-quarter track record from September 2023 through September 2026 shows both rapid scale-up and recent European drag [1]. Quarterly sales doubled from ₹302 crore in Sep 2023 (₹55 Cr EBITDA, 18% OPM, ₹0.86 EPS) to ₹576 crore in Mar 2025 (₹178 Cr EBITDA, 31% OPM, ₹4.79 EPS) [1]. March 2025 marked the consolidated margin peak [1]. Sales later reached ₹599 crore in Mar 2026 and ₹602 crore in Sep 2026 [1]. Year-on-year sales growth peaked at +74% in Jun 2024 and +42% in Sep 2024 on a low base, then eased to +19% YoY in Sep 2026 [1]. Consolidated OPM fell from 27% in Dec 2025 to 21% in Jun 2026 and 22% in Sep 2026 (EPS ₹2.51 and ₹3.19) [1][5][6]. Huron's French export-control drag offset India's 28% standalone margin [1][5][6].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated Profit & Loss Statement (Mar 2019 – TTM Sep 2026, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue scaled 3.9x from the FY21 trough (₹532 Cr) to FY26 (₹2,093 Cr) and ₹2,286 Cr TTM, while OPM expanded from 1.0% (FY20) to 25% (FY26); however, interest costs have climbed back to ₹82 Cr TTM.

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated Balance Sheet (Mar 2019 – Sep 2026, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Post-IPO equity reserves rebuilt from ₹12 Cr (Mar 2022) to ₹2,093 Cr (Sep 2026), yet borrowings tripled back from ₹304 Cr (Mar 2024) to ₹946 Cr (Sep 2026) alongside Other Assets surging to ₹2,989 Cr.

web_blocks.html: Balance-sheet growth from March 2023 to September 2026 shows the capital intensity behind that sales surge [1]. Total Assets more than doubled from ₹1,515 crore (Mar 2023) to ₹3,980 crore (Sep 2026) [1]. Fixed Assets plus Capital Work-in-Progress (CWIP) more than tripled from ₹298 crore (₹283 Cr + ₹15 Cr) in March 2023 to ₹975 crore (₹908 Cr + ₹67 Cr) in September 2026 as Rajkot expanded [1]. Meanwhile, Other Assets—mostly inventory and receivables—swelled from ₹1,214 crore to ₹2,989 crore [1]. That growth far outpaced Other Liabilities, which rose from ₹598 crore to ₹896 crore, forcing Borrowings back up to ₹946 crore [1].

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated Cash Flow Statement (Mar 2019 – Mar 2026, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Despite ₹803 Cr cumulative PAT over FY24–FY26, cumulative CFO was -₹99 Cr and cumulative Free Cash Flow was -₹847 Cr, funded by ₹937 Cr of net financing inflows.

web_blocks.caption: Working Capital & Return Ratios (Mar 2019 – Mar 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: ROCE recovered from -2% (FY20) to 21% (FY26), but Inventory Days jumped to 453 and Working Capital Days reached 234, keeping Cash Conversion Cycle near a full year (359 days).

web_blocks.html: Return on capital and payout discipline across all eight years confirm Jyoti CNC's capital-hungry model [1]. Consolidated ROCE swung from -2% (FY20) and -0% (FY21) to 5% (FY22), 8% (FY23), 21% (FY24), 24% (FY25), and 21% (FY26) [1]. High-utilization upcycles clearly produce strong accounting returns on capital [1]. Yet dividend payout stayed at 0% in every year (0.00% dividend yield) [1]. Jyoti reinvested 100% of retained profits—plus ₹937 crore of net financing inflows across FY24–FY26—into Rajkot capacity and working capital [1]. Investing Cash Flow totaled -₹170 Cr in FY24, -₹329 Cr in FY25, and -₹302 Cr in FY26 [1].

web_blocks.title: Price-Blind Fundamental Synthesis: Four-Point Graduation Checklist

web_blocks.html: Judged purely on business fundamentals—without reference to share price or valuation—Jyoti CNC earns a CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL quality verdict with PASS_WITH_WATCH KPI health. Its standalone engineering base, 5-axis leadership, captive foundry, 21.3% ROCE, 18.2% ROE, and ₹5,082 crore order book are clear strengths [1][4][5]. Still, the business must clear four operational hurdles before it can earn compounder status:

1. Inventory Normalization: Cut Inventory Days from 453 days toward <280–300 days as controller lead times ease and aerospace WIP ships [1][6]. 2. Cash Conversion Discipline: Lift pre-tax CFO/EBITDA from 34% (FY26) above 65% so operating cash funds capex without new debt [1]. 3. Balance-Sheet Debt Reduction: Reverse the post-IPO debt climb from ₹946 crore (Sep 2026) downward once the 16,000-machine Rajkot expansion ends [1][12]. 4. Huron Resolution: Resolve the French dual-use export probe, clear ~₹60 crore of unbooked H1 dispatches, and restore Huron Graffenstaden to breakeven [6][8].

book_paragraphs: When you and I step back and lay all eight years of Jyoti CNC's consolidated numbers side by side on the table—from March 2019 through September 2026—the story loses all ambiguity. This is not a quiet, steady, toll-booth compounder. It is a classic, high-beta precision capital-goods franchise with extraordinary engineering upside and equally real balance-sheet demands.

Look at the annual P&L arc first. From FY20 through FY23, Jyoti lost money four years in a row—a cumulative ₹180 crore in net losses—as sales fell from ₹965 crore to ₹532 crore and ₹71–90 crore of annual interest ate every rupee of operating profit. Then came the post-pandemic manufacturing renaissance and the January 2024 IPO: annual sales rocketed to ₹1,338 crore in FY24, ₹1,818 crore in FY25, ₹2,093 crore in FY26, and ₹2,286 crore on a trailing twelve-month basis. Operating margins jumped from 1.0% in FY20 to 25% in FY26, and ROCE rebounded to 21.3% alongside an 18.2% ROE.

Trace the 13-quarter rhythm from September 2023 to September 2026 and you can see both the operating power and the European friction in real time. Quarterly revenue doubled from ₹302 crore in September 2023—when earnings per share were just ₹0.86—to ₹602 crore in September 2026. Year-on-year sales growth surged to +74% in June 2024 before settling into a steadier +19% pace by September 2026. Consolidated operating margins peaked at 31% in March 2025 on ₹576 crore of sales, lifting quarterly EPS to ₹4.79. Yet in June and September 2026, consolidated margins compressed back to 21% and 22% (EPS ₹2.51 and ₹3.19) even as standalone India margins hit 28%, dragged down by Huron's Strasbourg losses and deferred revenue.

Now look at the balance sheet and cash flow tables right beside the P&L. Equity reserves grew from a precarious ₹12 crore in March 2022 to ₹2,093 crore in September 2026, thanks to the ₹1,000 crore fresh equity raise and ₹803 crore of retained profits. Yet Fixed Assets plus Capital Work-in-Progress more than tripled from ₹298 crore in March 2023 to ₹975 crore in September 2026 as Rajkot expanded toward 16,000 machines. Simultaneously, Other Assets—primarily inventory and receivables—swelled from ₹1,214 crore to ₹2,989 crore, while Total Assets more than doubled to ₹3,980 crore.

That asset bloat is why ₹803 crore of three-year net profit translated into minus ₹99 crore of operating cash flow and minus ₹847 crore of free cash flow, funded by ₹937 crore of net financing inflows. And that is why borrowings, after dropping to ₹304 crore right after the IPO, have marched steadily back up to ₹946 crore by September 2026, pushing trailing twelve-month interest back up to ₹82 crore.

Notice also that Jyoti pays zero dividends—0.00% yield and 0% payout across every single year from FY19 through FY26—because every rupee of internal profit, plus ₹937 crore of net financing inflows over FY24–FY26, has been plowed back into Rajkot machinery (Investing Cash Flow of -₹170 crore, -₹329 crore, and -₹302 crore across those three years), ECMS electronics, and working capital. Look at the ROCE arc across that span: from minus 2% in FY20 and 0% in FY21, it recovered to 5% in FY22, 8% in FY23, 21% in FY24, 24% in FY25, and 21% in FY26. In a capital-goods upcycle, reinvesting at 21.3% ROCE can build formidable scale; in a downcycle, ₹946 crore of debt and 453-day inventory become heavy baggage.

That is why our four-point graduation checklist is not academic nitpicking—it is the exact operational scorecard that separates a cyclical machine-tool boom from a durable industrial compounder. Every quarter from here, track Inventory Days, pre-tax CFO-to-EBITDA conversion, total borrowings, and Huron's Strasbourg bottom line before assuming the cycle has permanently changed.

Walk through those four checkpoints one by one so you know exactly what to look for in upcoming filings. First, watch Inventory Days: they need to glide down from 453 days toward under 280 to 300 days as controller lead times ease and aerospace work-in-progress ships out the door. Second, watch Cash Flow from Operations: pre-tax CFO-to-EBITDA must climb from 34% in FY26 above 65%, proving that accounting profits are finally turning into real bank cash.

Third, watch total borrowings: once Rajkot's 16,000-machine capex finishes, debt needs to start stepping down from ₹946 crore rather than climbing every quarter. Fourth, watch Strasbourg: Huron Graffenstaden must clear its ~₹60 crore of deferred H1 dispatches, resolve the French dual-use export probe without crippling sanctions, and stop bleeding ₹43 crore a quarter. Clear all four hurdles, and Jyoti CNC earns the right to be judged as a true compounder; stumble on them, and the cyclicality we saw in FY20–FY23 remains an ever-present threat.

With this eight-year price-blind foundation locked in—the Rajkot-to-Strasbourg origin story, the four customer end-markets, the profit-to-cash chasm, the 5-axis moat, the Huron governance audit, and the full FY19–Sep 2026 financial record—we are finally ready to turn to Pass 2 and weigh what the market is charging for this exact set of strengths and risks.

So where does that leave us at the end of our price-blind audit? Respect the machine-building craft, respect the ₹5,082 crore order book, and respect the 28% standalone EBITDA margins—but respect the cash flow statement even more. Jyoti CNC is a CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL franchise on PASS_WITH_WATCH KPI health. Until inventory days come down from 453 toward under 300, operating cash flow converts at least 65% of EBITDA, debt stops climbing from ₹946 crore, and Huron's Strasbourg cloud lifts, this remains a business you monitor with sharp forensic discipline rather than blind faith.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Eight years of numbers leave one unmistakable takeaway: Jyoti CNC has proven it can build world-class 5-axis machines and grow revenue nearly fourfold off a cycle trough. What it has not yet proven—and what Pass 2 will weigh against its market valuation—is whether it can fund that growth out of internal cash flow without endlessly tapping debt or equity.

book_callouts.title: THE FOUR-POINT GRADUATION CHECKLIST
book_callouts.text: Before Jyoti CNC can ever be treated as a steady compounder, track four numbers every quarter: Inventory Days moving down from 453 toward under 300, CFO-to-EBITDA rising from 34% toward 65%+, Borrowings declining from ₹946 crore, and Huron Graffenstaden returning to breakeven.

book_callouts.title: WHY ZERO DIVIDENDS MAKE SENSE—FOR NOW
book_callouts.text: A 0% dividend payout is appropriate while Jyoti is expanding from 6,000 to 16,000 machines and funding ECMS electronics. The test is whether that retained capital eventually produces positive Free Cash Flow instead of permanently higher borrowings.
